name: Bhatri
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.note: Nothing; ethnographic handbook. Only says the mother tongue Bhatri is 'a semi-autonomous dialect of Indo-Aryan family with an established tribal identity'.
Nothing; no phonology section, no descriptive sources cited.

sources.citation: Mahapatra, B. P. (ed.) 2002. Linguistic Survey of India: Orissa. Kolkata: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General. Bhatri mother-tongue sketch by Tapati Ghosh, printed pp. 136-150 (phonology pp. 137-140; PDF pp. 157-171, offset +21).
sources.note: Nothing. Phonology covers 5 vowels, one suprasegmental ('Supra segmental: Nasalization / ~ / of vowel is phonemic', p. 137; 'Supra-segmental phoneme / ~ / occurs more medially than initially and finally', p. 138), 28 consonants, allophones, diphthongs, clusters, syllable structure, morphophonemics; no stress, accent, intonation or pitch statement anywhere in the Bhatri chapter (grep of the whole chapter). The Sambalpuri chapter in the same volume has a Stress paragraph ('Stress in Sambalpuri does not appear to be phonemic... the initial syllable of each breath group bears stress'), which is S…

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. 1903. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. V Part II: Indo-Aryan Family, Eastern Group: Specimens of the Bihari and Oriya languages. Calcutta. Bhatri section pp. 484-486ff.
sources.note: Nothing for Bhatri: the section is a classification note (Bhatri 'is really a corrupt form of Oriya, with a few Marathi and Chattisgarhi forms'), census figures, a remark that 'this dialect omits aspirates', and the Prodigal Son specimen from Bastar in Devanagari. The general Oriya introduction (pp. 369-370) says that in 'true Oriya... the accent is put on the penultimate syllable if it is a long one and [never] further back than the antepenultimate' -- a statement about standard Oriya [ory], not Bhatri.
